key_individuals.name: The East India Company (EIC)
key_individuals.role: Joint-Stock Trading Monopoly That Became Territorial Ruler of Bengal
key_individuals.origins: Granted a royal monopoly charter by Queen Elizabeth I on New Year’s Eve 1600 after 218 London merchants pooled £68,000 for James Lancaster’s spice voyage (earning 300%+ profits).
key_individuals.significance: Grew from fortified coastal warehouses ("factories" at Surat, Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta) guarded by sepoy infantry into a private corporate empire collecting taxes over 20 million people in Bengal after 1765—whose unbending revenue demands worsened the catastrophic 1770 Bengal Famine (10 million deaths) and whose 1773 Tea Act sparked the Boston Tea Party.
achievements: Established fortified trading factories across Mughal coastlines following Sir Thomas Roe’s 1615–19 embassy to Emperor Jahangir.
Defeated Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey (1757) and acquired the sovereign Diwani tax-collection right across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa under the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad.
Granted a direct colonial tea monopoly under Parliament’s May 1773 Tea Act to clear 18 million pounds of unsold London tea, triggering the December 1773 Boston Tea Party.

key_individuals.name: Sir Thomas Roe
key_individuals.role: English Royal Ambassador to the Mughal Court of Emperor Jahangir (1615–1619)
key_individuals.origins: English diplomat dispatched by King James I in 1615 to the fabulously wealthy court of Mughal Emperor Jahangir when Mughal India produced over a quarter of global manufacturing.
key_individuals.significance: Negotiated imperial permission (farman) for English merchants to establish permanent trading "factories" at Surat—marking the peaceful, deferential commercial phase of Anglo-Mughal relations a century and a half before Plassey.
achievements: Attended Emperor Jahangir’s court (1615–19) as official ambassador of King James I.
Secured Mughal authorisation for fortified English warehouse depots at Surat in exchange for European silver bullion and novelties.

key_individuals.name: Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah
key_individuals.origins: Twenty-three-year-old ruler of wealthy Mughal Bengal who ordered the East India Company in 1756 to stop mounting unauthorised heavy cannons around Fort William in Calcutta.
key_individuals.significance: Captured Fort William with 50,000 troops in June 1756 (followed by the "Black Hole" guardroom deaths sensationalised in Britain), before being overthrown at the Battle of Plassey on 23 June 1757 when his general Mir Jafar accepted Robert Clive’s secret bribes.
achievements: Marched 50,000 soldiers to seize Calcutta’s Fort William (1756) to defend Bengali sovereignty against illegal Company fortifications.
Betrayed at Plassey (23 June 1757) when Mir Jafar held Bengal’s main divisions motionless and monsoon rain soaked Siraj’s uncovered cannon powder.

key_individuals.name: Robert Clive (1st Baron Clive)
key_individuals.role: East India Company Commander & Architect of Company Rule in Bengal
key_individuals.origins: Ambitious East India Company officer dispatched to recapture Calcutta in 1757, who combined military calculation with secret political bribery.
key_individuals.significance: Bribed Bengali commander Mir Jafar to win the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) and forced defeated Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II to sign the August 1765 Treaty of Allahabad—handing the Company the Diwani tax revenues of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
achievements: Used secret gold promises and tarpaulin-shielded artillery during a monsoon storm to defeat Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey (23 June 1757) and install Mir Jafar as puppet Nawab.
Secured the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad from Emperor Shah Alam II, turning a London trading company into a territorial tax-collecting state.

key_individuals.name: The Royal African Company (RAC)
key_individuals.role: Stuart Royal Slave-Trading Monopoly on the West African Coast
key_individuals.origins: Chartered by King Charles II in 1672 and headed by his brother James, Duke of York, to monopolise English trafficking along the West African coast within the Atlantic Triangular Trade.
key_individuals.significance: Demonstrated direct Stuart Crown and City involvement in transatlantic chattel slavery—imprisoning kidnapped Africans in fortified coastal dungeons (headquartered at Cape Coast Castle), branding captives "RAC" on the chest, and shipping tens of thousands across the deadly eight-week Middle Passage (where roughly one in six died, alongside atrocities such as the 1781 Zong massacre of 133 captives).
achievements: Operated armed West African slave forts exchanging British guns, iron bars, brass pans, and textiles for human captives.
Paved the way for Britain’s 1713 Spanish Asiento contract making Liverpool and Bristol Europe’s dominant slave-trading ports.

key_individuals.name: Olaudah Equiano
key_individuals.role: Freed African Author & Leading British Abolitionist Campaigner
key_individuals.origins: Enslaved as a boy in West Africa, carried across the Middle Passage, and later able to purchase his freedom through maritime trade before settling in London as a prominent voice in the Sons of Africa.
key_individuals.significance: Published his bestselling 1789 autobiography The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano—providing powerful firsthand African testimony alongside the 1788 Brookes ship diagram, Granville Sharp’s exposure of the 1781 Zong case, and Josiah Wedgwood’s medallion to propel Parliament toward the 1807 Abolition of the Slave Trade Act.
achievements: Published nine editions of his bestselling 1789 autobiography during his lifetime and toured Britain lecturing against the slave trade.
Helped transform British public opinion ahead of the landmark Abolition Act of 1807.

key_individuals.name: Queen Nanny of the Maroons
key_individuals.role: Asante Military & Spiritual Leader of the Windward Jamaican Maroons
key_individuals.origins: Leader of self-liberated Windward Maroon communities in Jamaica’s rugged Blue Mountains after Africans escaped Spanish and British sugar plantations following Cromwell’s 1655 seizure of Jamaica.
key_individuals.significance: Defeated heavily armed British regiments using forest leaf camouflage, cow-horn abeng signals, and mountain guerrilla ambushes—forcing British Governor Edward Trelawny to sign the 1739 Maroon peace treaties recognizing Maroon freedom and 1,500 sovereign acres.
achievements: Trained Maroon fighters in living-branch camouflage, abeng horn communication, and mountain ambush warfare alongside communal crop farming.
Forced Britain to negotiate the 1739 peace treaties acknowledging Maroon liberty and land (albeit containing the painful clause requiring Maroons to return future plantation runaways).

key_individuals.name: King George III
key_individuals.role: British Monarch During the Loss of the Thirteen American Colonies (1760–1820)
key_individuals.origins: Crowned in 1760 near the close of the Seven Years’ War, which left Great Britain victorious over France yet burdened with an enormous £133 million imperial war debt.
key_individuals.significance: Issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763 barring colonial settlement west of the Appalachians and backed parliamentary colonial taxation (1765 Stamp Act, 1773 Tea Act) and the punitive 1774 Coercive Acts after the Boston Tea Party—driving the Thirteen Colonies into the 1775–83 War of Independence.
achievements: Established the 1763 Proclamation Line and supported Quartering Acts and colonial duties to pay Seven Years’ War debts.

Responded to the 16 December 1773 destruction of 342 tea chests (£10,000) in Boston Harbour with the 1774 Coercive Acts closing Boston Port, culminating in British defeat at Saratoga (1777) and Yorktown (1781) and the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

key_individuals.name: Thomas Jefferson & George Washington
key_individuals.role: Author of the 1776 Declaration of Independence & Continental Army Commander
key_individuals.origins: Virginian Patriot leaders who challenged British "taxation without representation" after Lexington (April 1775) and Thomas Paine’s Common Sense (January 1776)—while both personally enslaving hundreds of African Americans.
key_individuals.significance: Jefferson drafted the July 1776 Declaration of Independence proclaiming "all men are created equal" (despite 41 of 56 signatories owning enslaved people), and Washington—aided by King Louis XVI’s French fleet after Saratoga (1777)—besieged Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown on 19 October 1781 to win US independence in 1783.
achievements: Jefferson authored the 4 July 1776 Declaration of Independence asserting natural rights to life and liberty while leaving chattel slavery intact.
Washington trapped 8,000 British regulars under Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown (October 1781) alongside French Admiral de Grasse’s Chesapeake naval blockade.

key_individuals.name: Lord Dunmore’s Ethiopian Regiment & The Black Loyalists
key_individuals.role: Enslaved African Americans Who Fought for the British Crown to Win Freedom
key_individuals.origins: Launched in November 1775 when Virginia’s Royal Governor Lord Dunmore issued a proclamation promising freedom to Patriot-owned enslaved people who crossed British lines to bear arms for King George III.
key_individuals.significance: Exposed the stark paradox of the American Revolution: thousands of enslaved men and women sought liberty with the British Army, and in 1783 British commander Sir Guy Carleton registered 3,000 Black Loyalists in the Book of Negroes at New York to sail free to Nova Scotia (and later found Freetown, Sierra Leone).
achievements: Thousands escaped rebel plantations following Lord Dunmore’s November 1775 Proclamation and later British emancipation promises.
In 1783, 3,000 Black Loyalists received British freedom certificates ("Birch Certificates") recorded in the Book of Negroes and evacuated from New York to Nova Scotia.

guided_reading.source_type_label: True Historical Story · Mughal Court to Plassey
guided_reading.book_title: The Velvet Coach & The Red Silk Tent: Sir Thomas Roe (1616) and Clive’s Diwani (1765)
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub · Grounded in Sir Thomas Roe’s Journal (BL Add MS 6115) & Clive’s 1765 Dispatches
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original narrative micro-history grounded in Ambassador Sir Thomas Roe’s 1616 Ajmer court journal and Robert Clive’s August–September 1765 Allahabad Treaty records.
guided_reading.author_context: When English ships first reached India after 1600, the Mughal Empire produced roughly a quarter of the world’s goods and dwarfed Stuart England in wealth. Tracing the arc from Sir Thomas Roe’s humble gift at Emperor Jahangir’s court in 1616 to Robert Clive’s seizure of Bengal’s taxes in 1765 reveals how a London trading company turned itself into a territorial empire.
guided_reading.cover_caption: Portrait of Sir Thomas Roe (after Michiel Jansz. van Mierevelt, c. 1640, National Portrait Gallery NPG 1354), English ambassador sent by King James I to the Mughal court of Emperor Jahangir.

vocabVault.def: Fourth Mughal Emperor (r. 1605–1627), whose dazzling court at Ajmer received English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe.
An official Mughal imperial decree granting foreign merchants permission to trade at coastal ports like Surat.
Indian infantry soldiers recruited, drilled, and paid by the British East India Company.
The 1765 right to collect all land taxes across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa—turning the East India Company into Bengal’s ruler.

guided_reading.extract:
In January 1616, English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe bowed low inside the marble palace of Mughal Emperor Jahangir at Ajmer. Mughal India then produced nearly a quarter of the world’s textiles and riches. Jahangir sat glittering in ropes of pearls and rubies larger than walnuts. Hoping to impress the Emperor, Roe presented a wooden English coach lined with crimson velvet.

Jahangir smiled politely, rode once around the palace courtyard by torchlight, and handed the coach to his royal craftsmen. Within weeks, Indian builders produced a finer copy upholstered in gleaming silver brocade. Humbled by Mughal wealth and horsemen, Roe warned the East India Company in London: "If you will profit, seek it at sea, and in quiet trade." English merchants survived solely by the Emperor’s firman—his written permission.

One hundred and forty-nine years later, that world had turned upside down. As Mughal authority fractured after 1707, the Company drilled private armies of Indian sepoys armed with flintlock muskets. After bribing rival general Mir Jafar to win the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive met young Emperor Shah Alam II inside a red silk tent at Allahabad in August 1765. Perched atop a covered dining table as a makeshift throne, Clive took the Diwani—the legal right to collect taxes from twenty million people in Bengal. Without shipping an ounce of English silver, humble spice traders had become corporate kings.

parent_discussion.question: What happened when Ambassador Sir Thomas Roe tried to impress Emperor Jahangir with a velvet English coach in 1616?
parent_discussion.answer: Emperor Jahangir rode it once by torchlight and handed it to his royal craftsmen, who within weeks built an even finer copy lined in gleaming silver brocade.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Sir Thomas Roe warn the East India Company in 1616: 'If you will profit, seek it at sea, and in quiet trade'?
parent_discussion.answer: He was humbled by Mughal wealth, skilled craftsmen, and horsemen—India made nearly a quarter of the world’s textiles and riches, and English merchants survived solely by the Emperor’s written permission (a firman).

parent_discussion.question: Between 1616 and 1765, how had the balance of power between the Mughal Emperor and the East India Company completely flipped?
parent_discussion.answer: In 1616 English merchants had to bow at court and rely on the Emperor’s firman to trade, but after Mughal authority weakened, the Company used private sepoy armies and bribery at Plassey to take the Diwani—taxing twenty million people in Bengal themselves.

story_check.question: How did Emperor Jahangir’s court craftsmen respond to Sir Thomas Roe’s gift of an English velvet coach in 1616?
options: They burned it outside the palace gates
They built an even finer copy lined in silver brocade within weeks
They traded it to Portuguese sailors
They could not figure out how its wheels turned
story_check.feedback: Correct! Mughal artisans swiftly built a superior silver-brocade coach, reminding Roe how advanced Indian craftsmanship was.

story_check.question: What advice did Sir Thomas Roe send back to the East India Company in 1616?
options: March immediately on Delhi with cannons
Abandon Asia and sail only to Virginia
Seek profit at sea and in quiet trade rather than land wars
Refuse to bow to the Mughal Emperor
story_check.feedback: Spot on. Humbled by Mughal wealth and horsemen, Roe told the Company to seek profit at sea and in quiet trade.

story_check.question: What massive power passed to Robert Clive and the East India Company inside the tent at Allahabad in August 1765?
options: The Diwani—collecting land taxes from 20 million people in Bengal
Ownership of the port of Liverpool
A monopoly on North American fur trading
story_check.feedback: Exactly right. Winning the Diwani turned a London trading company into the tax-collecting ruler of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

monday_cold_call.question: Contrast 1616 with 1765: what happened to Sir Thomas Roe’s velvet coach at Ajmer, and what did Robert Clive win inside his tent at Allahabad?
monday_cold_call.answer: In 1616 Emperor Jahangir’s craftsmen outdid Roe’s coach in silver brocade while England begged to trade; in 1765 Clive seized the Bengal Diwani to tax 20 million Indians.

Think: Why did Sir Thomas Roe need an imperial firman just to trade at Surat in 1616?

Pair: Trace what changed between 1707 and 1765 to let a London company seize Bengal.

guided_reading.book_title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano: Below Decks (1789)
guided_reading.author: Olaudah Equiano (Chapter II, London, 1789 • Calibrated for Aloud Reading)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Sentence-calibrated for Year 8 aloud reading from Chapter II of Olaudah Equiano’s 1789 London autobiography (BL 615.d.11), preserving Equiano’s first-person voice and vocabulary.
guided_reading.author_context: Olaudah Equiano (c. 1745–1797)—known for much of his life as Gustavus Vassa—survived enslavement, bought his own freedom for forty pounds in 1766, and helped lead the 'Sons of Africa' abolitionist campaign in London. Published in 1789 just as MPs debated the slave trade, his bestselling memoir shattered pro-slavery myths with unforgettable eyewitness truth.
guided_reading.cover_caption: Abolitionist stowage diagram of the Liverpool slave ship Brookes under the Regulated Slave Trade Act of 1788, showing 454 enslaved men, women, and boys packed into decks barely 2 feet 7 inches high.

vocabVault.def: Formerly enslaved writer and London abolitionist whose 1789 autobiography exposed the horrors of the Middle Passage.
The brutal six-to-twelve-week Atlantic voyage carrying enslaved Africans in chains to plantations in the Americas.
A legal system treating human beings and their children as permanent private property ('cargo') to be bought and sold.
Extreme greed for money—the moral crime Equiano blamed for slave traders cramming captives below decks to die.

guided_reading.extract:
"The first object that met my eyes when I reached the coast was the sea, and a slave ship riding at anchor. Sight of that vessel filled me with astonishment, which quickly turned to terror when I was carried on board. Rough sailors immediately handled and tossed me up to check whether I was sound and strong. Looking around at their strange faces and a boiling copper pot on deck, I felt sure I had entered a world of bad spirits who meant to kill me.

Soon I was forced down beneath the wooden decks. There a dreadful stench struck my nostrils such as I had never known in my life. Overcome by the foul air and the weeping all around me, I grew so sick and low that I could not swallow a bite of food. Two crewmen tied my hands and flogged me severely because I refused to eat.

Down in the hold, the fierce tropical heat and the crushing crowd nearly suffocated us. Chained captives had scarcely room to turn, and heavy sweat poured from every body until the air became unfit to breathe. Deadly sickness soon swept through the ship, killing many poor souls who fell victim to the short-sighted greed—the avarice—of their purchasers. The shrieks of the women and the groans of the dying made the whole hold a scene of horror almost beyond belief."

parent_discussion.question: When young Olaudah Equiano was first carried onto the slave ship, what made him feel sure he had entered a world of 'bad spirits'?
parent_discussion.answer: Rough sailors immediately handled and tossed him up to check whether he was strong, and seeing their strange faces and a boiling copper pot on deck terrified him into thinking they meant to kill him.

parent_discussion.question: Why did two crewmen tie Equiano’s hands and flog him when grief and sickness stopped him from eating?
parent_discussion.answer: Under chattel slavery, traders treated enslaved people as private property ('cargo') to be sold on plantations in the Americas, so the crew forced captives to stay alive for profit rather than out of kindness.

parent_discussion.question: Equiano blames the deaths below decks on the 'short-sighted greed—the avarice—of their purchasers.' Why does he call that greed 'short-sighted'?
parent_discussion.answer: By cramming chained captives into suffocating tropical heat with scarcely room to turn, the traders’ own greed bred deadly sickness that killed many of the very people they planned to sell.

story_check.question: What did the slave-ship crew immediately do when young Olaudah Equiano was carried onto the deck?
options: Handled and tossed him to test whether his body was strong
Allowed him to stay on the upper deck for the voyage
Taught him to steer the ship’s wheel
story_check.feedback: Correct! Sailors inspected and tossed captives like marketplace goods before forcing them below decks.

story_check.question: Why did the air below decks become 'unfit to breathe' during the Atlantic crossing?
options: Cold Arctic snow blocked the hatches
Coal smoke leaked from a steam engine
Crushing overcrowding, tropical heat, sweat, and filth suffocated chained captives
The ship carried barrels of gunpowder
story_check.feedback: Spot on. Packing hundreds of chained people into low, unventilated timber holds bred suffocating heat and deadly epidemics.

story_check.question: What moral flaw in the slave traders ('purchasers') did Equiano blame for so many deaths on board?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right. Equiano named 'avarice'—ruthless greed—as the cause of cramming human beings into deadly holds.

monday_cold_call.question: What word meaning 'extreme greed' did Olaudah Equiano use to explain why so many captives died below decks—and what conditions did he describe in the hold?
monday_cold_call.answer: Equiano blamed the purchasers’ 'avarice'; he described chained captives packed with scarcely room to turn in fierce tropical heat, foul air, and deadly sickness.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: How did Olaudah Equiano gain his freedom in 1766, and what London group did he help lead?

Pair: Cross-reference Equiano’s memories of the hold with the 1788 Brookes stowage plan—how did word and image work together in 1789?

Share: Why was Black abolitionist leadership essential alongside Parliamentary campaigners in ending the British slave trade?

Why was Equiano flogged below decks when he grew too sick to eat?

guided_reading.book_title: Sound of the Abeng: Queen Nanny, Mountain Camouflage & The 1739 Maroon Peace Treaty
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub · Grounded in Colonial Office CO 137/23 & Bryan Edwards (1796)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original narrative micro-history grounded in the 1739–1740 Jamaican Maroon Peace Treaties (TNA CO 137/23), Bryan Edwards’s 1796 military account, and Windward Maroon heritage records.
guided_reading.author_context: Enslaved Africans in Jamaica never accepted sugar-plantation bondage passively. Escaping into the razor-sharp limestone Cockpits and mist-covered Blue Mountains, Windward leader Queen Nanny and Leeward commander Captain Cudjoe waged such brilliant guerrilla warfare between 1728 and 1739 that the British Empire had to beg for peace.
guided_reading.cover_caption: John Seller’s hand-coloured map of Jamaica (Novissima et Accuratissima Insulae Jamaicae Descriptio, c. 1672–1675, Royal Museums Greenwich F8080), showing the Blue Mountains and interior parishes where Maroon communities defied British armies.

vocabVault.def: Self-liberated Africans and their descendants who escaped Caribbean plantations and defended free mountain towns.
A curved cow-horn trumpet blown by Jamaican Maroon lookouts to send coded warnings across miles of mountain valleys.
Fast hit-and-run ambushes using steep terrain, stealth, and leaf camouflage to defeat a larger regular army.
Asante-born military strategist and spiritual leader of the Windward Maroons in Jamaica’s Blue Mountains.

guided_reading.extract:
High in the mist-wrapped Blue Mountains of eastern Jamaica, British redcoats marched single-file along a narrow stone ledge. Sweat soaked their heavy red wool coats and clanking musket belts. Suddenly, a low, haunting note echoed from peak to peak. Far above them, a Maroon scout blew the curved cow-horn called the abeng to warn of the marching column.

Before the soldiers spotted a single face, the green forest wall seemed to move. Dressed from head to foot in tied branches and wild leaves, Windward Maroon fighters struck fast and vanished into deep limestone gullies. Their leader was Queen Nanny, a bold Asante-born leader who built Nanny Town high above sheer cliffs. There free families grew yams, plantains, and pumpkins far beyond any planter’s whip. In western Jamaica’s jagged Cockpit Country, Captain Cudjoe’s fighters broke British supply lines the same way.

By March 1739, eleven years of hard mountain fighting had exhausted the British garrison. Nearly a century before Britain ended slavery in 1833, Governor Edward Trelawny sent officers into the hills to beg for peace. Signed treaties recognised Maroon freedom forever and granted fifteen hundred acres of free land. Yet peace carried a bitter price. To keep their hard-won liberty, Maroon chiefs had to promise to hand back future runaways from lowland sugar estates.

parent_discussion.question: Why were regular British soldiers in scarlet uniforms repeatedly outfought in Jamaica’s Blue Mountains and Cockpit Country?
parent_discussion.answer: Heavy red wool uniforms made easy targets on narrow trails, while Maroon fighters knew every cliff, used head-to-foot leaf camouflage, and sent coded abeng horn alerts.

parent_discussion.question: Why was the March 1739 peace treaty such an extraordinary victory for Queen Nanny and the Maroons?
parent_discussion.answer: Nearly a century before Britain ended slavery in 1833, eleven years of mountain fighting forced Governor Trelawny to beg for peace and recognise Maroon freedom and 1,500 acres of free land.

parent_discussion.question: The 1739 peace treaty carried a 'bitter price'—why was the promise to return future runaways such an agonising choice for Maroon leaders?
parent_discussion.answer: Maroon chiefs secured permanent freedom and land for their mountain towns, but only by agreeing to hand back future escapees from lowland sugar estates so British troops would stop attacking them.

story_check.question: What instrument did Maroon lookouts blow to send coded military signals across Jamaica’s mountain valleys?
story_check.feedback: Correct! Maroon scouts blew the curved cow-horn called the abeng to send coded warnings across miles of mountain valleys.

story_check.question: Which brilliant strategist led the Windward Maroons from their cliffside stronghold in the Blue Mountains?
story_check.feedback: Spot on. Asante-born leader Queen Nanny built Nanny Town high above the cliffs and led the Windward Maroons in the Blue Mountains.

story_check.question: What was the outcome of the eleven years of mountain fighting in Jamaica by March 1739?
options: Britain signed treaties recognising Maroon freedom and 1,500 acres of land, alongside a harsh runaway-return promise
Sugar plantations were outlawed across the Caribbean
The Maroons sailed to Nova Scotia
story_check.feedback: Exactly right. Exhausted by Maroon guerrilla tactics, Governor Trelawny signed treaties recognising Maroon freedom and 1,500 acres of land, but demanded they return future runaways.

monday_cold_call.question: How did Queen Nanny’s Windward Maroons use the abeng and jungle terrain to defeat British redcoats—and what difficult compromise sat inside the 1739 treaty?
monday_cold_call.answer: Lookouts blew coded warnings on the abeng horn while leaf-camouflaged fighters ambushed redcoats in steep ravines; the 1739 treaty secured Maroon freedom and land, but required returning future plantation runaways.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Look at Seller’s 1672 map of Jamaica—how did the island’s mountain spine aid Maroon survival?

Pair: Weigh what the Maroons WON in 1739 against what Governor Trelawny demanded in return.

Share: How does Queen Nanny’s victory challenge the old myth that freedom was simply 'gifted' from Westminster?

How did Maroon fighters use Jamaica’s terrain and foliage against British soldiers?
What did the Maroons gain—and what compromise did Britain demand—in the 1739 treaty?

guided_reading.book_title: Tyranny & Tea Chests: Phillis Wheatley’s Verse (1772) and George Hewes at Boston Harbour
guided_reading.author: Phillis Wheatley (Poems, 1773) & Shoemaker George Robert Twelves Hewes (1773 Eyewitness)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Verbatim lines from Phillis Wheatley’s October 1772 poem 'To the Right Honourable William, Earl of Dartmouth' (published London, 1773) paired with Boston shoemaker George Hewes’s eyewitness account of 16 December 1773.
guided_reading.author_context: After the Seven Years’ War doubled Britain’s debt, Westminster taxed American newspapers (1765 Stamp Act) and granted the East India Company a colonial tea monopoly (1773). In rebellious Boston, enslaved poet Phillis Wheatley exposed the sharp irony of slaveholding colonists crying 'Tyranny!'—months before shoemaker George Hewes helped dump 342 tea chests into the harbour.
guided_reading.cover_caption: William Bradford’s Pennsylvania Journal woodcut (31 October 1765), printing a skull and crossbones ('This is the Place to affix the STAMP') in protest against the British Stamp Act.

vocabVault.def: Enslaved African-born Boston teenager who in 1773 became the first African American author to publish a book of poetry.
Cruel, unchecked rule without consent—linked by Wheatley to her own kidnapping from West Africa.
Colonial protest networks of artisans, dockworkers, and merchants who organised boycotts and the 1773 Boston Tea Party.
Exclusive control of a trade—Parliament’s 1773 Tea Act let the East India Company undercut local colonial merchants.

guided_reading.extract:
In Boston in October 1772, white colonists cried out that London taxes without elected MPs turned freeborn Britons into "slaves." Watching from a Boston house where she herself was legally enslaved, nineteen-year-old poet Phillis Wheatley wrote to King George III’s minister, the Earl of Dartmouth.
Should you, my lord, while you peruse my song,
Wonder from whence my love of Freedom sprung?
I, young in life, by seeming cruel fate
Was snatch’d from Afric’s fancy’d happy seat.
What pangs excruciating must molest,
What sorrows labour in my parent’s breast?
And can I then but pray
Others may never feel tyrannic sway?
Fourteen months later, on the freezing night of 16 December 1773, Boston’s tax anger boiled over at Griffin’s Wharf. Poor shoemaker George Hewes slipped into a blacksmith’s shop, rubbed black coal dust over his face and hands, and gripped a small hatchet. Dressed as Mohawk warriors, he and the Sons of Liberty boarded three East India Company ships in dead silence. In three hours, they chopped open three hundred and forty-two chests of Company tea and heaved them into the harbour. Salt water turned brown with floating leaves from Bengal and China. Not one man was allowed to pocket a single ounce for himself.

parent_discussion.question: How did nineteen-year-old Phillis Wheatley explain where her deep 'love of Freedom' came from in her 1772 poem?
parent_discussion.answer: She explained that she had been snatched as a child from Africa—causing unbearable sorrow to her parents—so she prayed others would never suffer 'tyrannic sway.'

parent_discussion.question: Why did George Hewes and the Sons of Liberty smear coal dust on their faces yet forbid anyone from stealing a single ounce of tea?
parent_discussion.answer: Disguises hid their identities from British arrest, while strict discipline proved they were staging a principled tax protest—not a greedy dockside robbery.

parent_discussion.question: White colonists in Boston claimed British taxes turned them into 'slaves'—why did nineteen-year-old Phillis Wheatley’s poem make that claim sound so striking and uncomfortable?
parent_discussion.answer: Wheatley was legally enslaved right there in Boston after being kidnapped from West Africa, so her poem highlighted the huge gap between paying unfair taxes and actually losing your freedom.

story_check.question: Why did Phillis Wheatley say she understood 'tyrannic sway' better than anyone in Boston?
options: She had paid heavy London taxes on tea
She had been kidnapped as a child from West Africa into slavery
She owned a Boston tea warehouse
She served in the Royal Navy
story_check.feedback: Correct! Snatched from West Africa as a young girl, Wheatley reminded British and colonial leaders alike what real loss of freedom meant.

story_check.question: How did shoemaker George Hewes disguise himself before boarding the tea ships on 16 December 1773?
options: In Mohawk dress with coal dust smeared on his face and hands
story_check.feedback: Spot on. Hewes stopped at a blacksmith’s shop to darken his face with coal dust and carried a small hatchet to split the wooden chests.

story_check.question: How many chests of East India Company tea were thrown into Boston Harbour during the three-hour raid?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right. Working in dead silence, George Hewes and the Sons of Liberty chopped open 342 chests of East India Company tea and dumped them into Boston Harbour.

monday_cold_call.question: How did enslaved poet Phillis Wheatley gently expose colonial hypocrisy in 1772—and why did George Hewes’s boarding party ban stealing any tea in 1773?
monday_cold_call.answer: Wheatley showed her love of freedom came from actually being kidnapped from Africa into slavery; Hewes’s Sons of Liberty banned theft to prove the Tea Party was a political protest, not looting.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why had Parliament taxed the Thirteen Colonies after 1763 in the first place?

Pair: Compare Phillis Wheatley’s view of 'Freedom' in 1772 with the Sons of Liberty’s slogan 'No taxation without representation'.

Share: How did Parliament’s furious 1774 punishment of Boston turn a tax protest into the American Revolution?

guided_reading.book_title: Memoirs of the Life of Boston King: From Charleston Bondage to the Book of Negroes
guided_reading.author: Boston King (The Methodist Magazine, London, 1798 • Calibrated for Aloud Reading)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Sentence-calibrated for Year 8 aloud reading from carpenter and preacher Boston King’s 1798 London memoir (The Methodist Magazine, March–June 1798).
guided_reading.author_context: While Thomas Jefferson’s 1776 Declaration of Independence proclaimed that 'all men are created equal', Jefferson himself enslaved over six hundred people. Judging that real freedom lay behind British lines under Lord Dunmore’s 1775 and Clinton’s 1779 proclamations, over 20,000 Black Loyalists—including South Carolina carpenter Boston King and his wife Violet—risked their lives to escape.
guided_reading.cover_caption: John Trumbull, Surrender of Lord Cornwallis (1820, US Capitol Rotunda), depicting the October 1781 British defeat at Yorktown that decided American independence.

vocabVault.def: Over 20,000 enslaved African Americans who escaped Patriot masters during the American Revolution to claim freedom with British forces.
The 1775 British offer promising immediate freedom to enslaved people owned by American Rebels if they crossed into British lines.
The official 1783 British military ledger registering 3,000 Black Loyalists evacuated as free people from New York to Nova Scotia.
The cold Atlantic province in Canada where Boston and Violet King settled as free citizens before later sailing to Sierra Leone.

guided_reading.extract:
"In 1780, British troops captured Charleston in South Carolina. Word ran fast across the plantations that freedom awaited all enslaved people who reached the King’s camp. Choosing to risk death rather than stay in chains, I borrowed a horse at midnight and rode past the Rebel patrols. British soldiers welcomed me as a free man, though deadly smallpox soon swept through our tents.

Yet when peace was signed with the United States in 1783, dreadful terror gripped every Black Loyalist in New York. Rumours ran down the alleys that all former slaves would be handed back to their old American masters! Worse still, angry Southern planters walked right into New York seizing men and women off the pavements. For days my wife Violet and I could neither eat nor sleep for fear of returning to chains.

Mercifully, British General Sir Guy Carleton kept the Crown’s promise to everyone who had served a full year. Clerks wrote our names, ages, and scars into a great ledger called the Book of Negroes. Holding our signed certificates of freedom, Violet and I boarded the ship L’Abondance and sailed free to Nova Scotia. Years later, we crossed the Atlantic once more to help build a free Black settlement in Sierra Leone."

parent_discussion.question: Why did Boston King risk his life riding past Rebel patrols to join the British camp in 1780?
parent_discussion.answer: Word had spread across South Carolina’s plantations that Britain promised freedom to enslaved people who reached the King’s camp, and he chose to risk death rather than stay in chains.

parent_discussion.question: Why was the 1783 peace treaty a moment of terror rather than celebration for Black Loyalists waiting in New York?
parent_discussion.answer: Rumours spread that former slaves would be handed back to their old American masters, and angry Southern planters walked into New York seizing people off the pavements—until General Sir Guy Carleton kept Britain’s promise and registered them in the Book of Negroes.

parent_discussion.question: Look at how closely Boston and Violet King held onto their signed certificates of freedom and later sailed all the way to Sierra Leone—what does their journey show about how fragile freedom felt in 1783?
parent_discussion.answer: Even after escaping to British lines, peace nearly saw them dragged back into slavery off New York’s streets, so written proof in the Book of Negroes and moving to free settlements in Nova Scotia and Sierra Leone were vital to protect their liberty.

story_check.question: How did Boston King escape his South Carolina plantation to reach British lines at Charleston in 1780?
options: He swam out to a French warship
He borrowed a horse at midnight and slipped past American patrols
His master paid for his train ticket
He hid inside a tea chest from Boston
story_check.feedback: Correct! Choosing to risk death rather than stay in chains, Boston King rode past Rebel patrols by night to claim British protection.

story_check.question: Why couldn’t Boston and Violet King eat or sleep in New York when peace was announced in 1783?
options: The city had run out of drinking water
They feared being handed back to American slaveholders who were seizing people off the streets
Spanish warships were bombarding the harbour
story_check.feedback: Spot on. Rumours spread that former slaves would be returned, and angry Southern planters were seizing people right off New York’s pavements.

story_check.question: What famous 1783 British ledger recorded 3,000 Black Loyalists with signed freedom certificates before they sailed for Nova Scotia?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right. General Sir Guy Carleton’s clerks registered 3,000 Black Loyalists—including Boston and Violet King—in the Book of Negroes.

monday_cold_call.question: Why did Boston King risk everything to reach British lines in 1780—and what document saved him and Violet in New York in 1783?
monday_cold_call.answer: Britain promised freedom to enslaved people who escaped Rebel masters to join the King’s camp; in 1783 being listed in the Book of Negroes with signed freedom certificates saved them from re-enslavement.

teacher_guidance_overview.curriculum_focus: KS3 National Curriculum: Ideas, political power, industry and empire: Britain, 1745–1901 (with seventeenth-century foundations in early colonial expansion, corporate empire in India, the transatlantic slave trade, African resistance, and the American Revolution).

teacher_guidance_overview.non_specialist_summary: This Year 8 unit examines the rise, human cost, and fracture of the First British Empire between 1600 and 1783. Pupils investigate how royal charters empowered private corporations—the East India Company in Mughal Bengal and the Royal African Company in West Africa—to build fortunes through military bribery and chattel slavery, how enslaved Africans resisted aboard ships, in Maroon strongholds under Queen Nanny, and as Black Loyalists, and why colonial taxation cost Britain the Thirteen American Colonies.
